value.overview: The Black-and-white Warbler (Mniotilta varia) is a striking New World warbler named for its bold black-and-white plumage. Unlike most warblers, it regularly creeps along tree trunks and large branches, using its strong claws and stiff tail to search bark and crevices for prey. It breeds in North America and migrates through or winters in Central America, including Costa Rica, where it is a familiar seasonal visitor in wooded habitats.
value.classification: The Black-and-white Warbler is the only species in the genus Mniotilta. It belongs to the Parulidae family, the New World warblers, within the order Passeriformes.
value.identification: Adults have sharply contrasting black-and-white striping on the head, back, wings, and underparts. Breeding males usually show a black throat, black cheek, and stronger facial markings, while females and immature birds have a paler, grayer appearance and a whitish throat. The species is readily recognized by its habit of moving deliberately up and down tree trunks like a nuthatch. Its thin, high-pitched song is often described as a squeaky or mechanical series of notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-and-white Warbler breeds across much of eastern and central North America and parts of southern Canada. During migration and winter it occurs from the southern United States through Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America. In Costa Rica it is a nonbreeding migrant rather than a resident breeder, and it can be found in lowland and foothill forest, cloud forest, riparian woodland, forest edges, gardens, parks, and shaded coffee plantations. It uses both mature and second-growth vegetation.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. Individuals reach Costa Rica during the nonbreeding season, with passage birds also occurring during spring and autumn migration; they depart northward to breed in North America.
value.breeding: Breeding takes place in mature deciduous or mixed forests, although second-growth woodland and swampy forest may also be used. The female generally builds a well-hidden cup nest on or near the ground, often beside a tree root, stump, log, or low vegetation. The nest is made from grasses, bark strips, leaves, and other plant material and is lined with finer materials. Both adults participate in raising the young, while the male commonly defends the breeding territory.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of insects and their larvae, spiders, and other small arthropods. The warbler searches methodically over bark, branches, foliage, and fallen woody material, often probing crevices or lifting loose bark. Its specialized climbing behavior allows it to exploit prey that many other warblers overlook. During migration and winter, it may also take small fruits or other available foods, but animal prey remains the principal food.
value.behavior: This species is an active but deliberate forager that usually moves alone or in mixed-species feeding flocks outside the breeding season. It creeps vertically along trunks and large limbs, frequently changing direction while inspecting the bark. Males are territorial on the breeding grounds and may also defend feeding areas in winter. The bird can be inconspicuous despite its bold pattern because it often stays close to trunks and shaded vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered stable overall, although local or regional declines may occur where forest habitat is lost or fragmented.
